newsitem.title: USA: FERC gives initial nod to Calif. power market plan.
newsitem.headline: FERC gives initial nod to Calif. power market plan.

text.p: California on Tuesday moved a few steps closer toward opening its electricity market to competition as the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission gave a preliminary nod to a power market plan by the state's big utilities.

California was the first state to submit a retail market plan to the FERC for approval, and is considered the bellwether for how the federal commission will react to several other states' moves toward customer choice.
"It behooves everyone to take a look at what California has proposed and how we have ruled on it," said Commissioner James Hoecker.
The commission said it hoped to issue a separate ruling before the end of the year on market power issues raised in the three utilities' plan, which was submitted last April.
It accepted their proposal to separate the ISO from the power exchange and charge access fees to recover their transmission costs and congestion fees to encourage efficient use of the system.

But the FERC said before the utilities could begin handing over their transmission facilities to the ISO, they would have to specify by March 31, 1997 exactly which facilities would be under the new operator's control and show how the transfer ensured that the utilities would no longer be able to dominate the power market.

The commission rejected the utilities' plan to limit the membership of the governing boards to California residents only. While not calling for a specific number of out-of-state members, the commission said the boards should represent any parties interested in a role in the California market.
"This will be a regional market and hopefully a regional ISO and PX (power exchange)," said Commissioner William Massey.

The commission also rejected a proposal to make a state oversight board the ultimate source of appeals for reviewing the ISO's decisions, because under federal law, the FERC is supposed to have exclusive jurisdiction over wholesale electricity transactions.
The utilities were told to answer questions raised by the FERC on how their plan would affect competition and transmission expansion in California.
"We think the ISO should have a more active role in expansion decisions," said Commissioner Vicky Bailey.

The commission also wanted the companies to explain how the FERC should deal with their demand that other states must give them direct access to their retail customers when California opens its retail market to all power producers. Under federal law, the commission is not allowed to order a state to open its retail electricity market.
